title: Palace of Westminster
blurb: The Palace of Westminster in London, meeting place of the UK Parliament, in simplified schematic form: nearly 300 m of Perpendicular Gothic Revival river frontage on the Thames, with the 98.5 m Victoria Tower, the 96.3 m Elizabeth Tower housing the Great Bell Big Ben, and the 91 m octagonal Central Tower.

sourceUrls.label: parliament.uk: House of Commons factsheet G11

systems.name: Towers
systems.description: The three principal towers: Victoria Tower at 98.5 m, Elizabeth Tower at 96.3 m and the octagonal Central Tower at 91 m, plus the three minor towers.

systems.name: Chambers and lobbies
systems.description: The two debating chambers with their benches, the division lobbies, the Members and Peers lobbies, and the Royal Apartments.

systems.name: Centre
systems.description: The octagonal Central Lobby below the Central Tower, with the corridors to each House and St Stephens Hall.

systems.name: Frontage and roofs
systems.description: The 265.8 m river frontage on the Thames, the Terrace, and the main roof with its chimney stacks.

systems.name: Westminster Hall
systems.description: The oldest structure on the estate, completed in 1099, with the largest medieval timber roof in Northern Europe.

systems.name: Courtyards and grounds
systems.description: The yards, courts and gardens inside and around the palace.

explanations.victoria tower: The Victoria Tower at the south-western corner of the palace, 98.5 m tall, the tallest part of the palace and the tallest secular building in the world when it was completed in 1858. Its base holds the Sovereigns Entrance with its 15 m archway, and its interior houses the Parliamentary Archives. Exact window divisions are schematic.
explanations.elizabeth tower: The Elizabeth Tower at the north end of the palace, 96.3 m tall, designed by Augustus Pugin and completed in 1859. Its four dials are 6.9 m across and the Great Bell, Big Ben, weighs 13.8 tonnes. Exact dial and spire detail is schematic.
explanations.central tower: The octagonal Central Tower over the middle of the palace, 91 m tall, the shortest of the three principal towers. It was added as a ventilation chimney and is the only palace tower with a stone spire. Exact profile is schematic.
explanations.speakers tower: Speakers Tower, the pavilion at the northern end of the river front, containing Speakers House. Exact massing is schematic.
explanations.chancellors tower: Chancellors Tower, the pavilion at the southern end of the river front. Exact massing is schematic.
explanations.st stephens tower: St Stephens Tower in the middle of the west front, housing the public entrance to the palace. Exact massing is schematic.
explanations.house of commons chamber: The Chamber of the House of Commons at the northern end of the palace, 14 by 20.7 m, opened in 1950 after the Victorian chamber was destroyed by German bombs in 1941. Its benches are green; the chamber seats only 427 of the 650 members.
explanations.house of lords chamber: The Chamber of the House of Lords in the southern part of the palace, 13.7 by 24.4 m, with red benches on three sides, the Sovereigns Throne under its gilded canopy, and the Woolsack.
explanations.members lobby: The Members Lobby, a cube of 13.7 m, where members of Parliament hold discussions and are interviewed by accredited journalists, collectively known as The Lobby.
explanations.peers lobby: The Peers Lobby north of the Lords Chamber, 12 m square and 10 m high, with a floor centrepiece of a radiant Tudor rose made of Derbyshire marbles.
explanations.royal apartments: The monarchs processional rooms at the southern end of the palace: the Norman Porch, the Robing Room with the Chair of State, the 33.5 m Royal Gallery and the Princes Chamber. Exact room layouts are schematic.
explanations.central lobby: The Central Lobby, originally named Octagon Hall, 18 m across and 23 m from the floor to the centre of the vaulted ceiling, directly below the Central Tower. It is the political heart of the palace and the origin of the term lobbying.
explanations.commons corridor: The Commons Corridor leading north from the Central Lobby toward the Members Lobby. Exact decoration is schematic.
explanations.peers corridor: The Peers Corridor leading south from the Central Lobby toward the Peers Lobby. Exact decoration is schematic.
explanations.st stephens hall: St Stephens Hall, the public route from St Stephens Entrance to the Central Lobby, with marble statues of prominent parliamentarians. Exact interior is schematic.
explanations.palace frontage: The palace frontage: 265.8 m of river front facing the Thames, 21.3 m to the roofline, with the north front 70.7 m and the south front 98.2 m, built of sand-coloured Anston limestone. Exact bay divisions are schematic.
explanations.river terrace: The River Terrace on the Thames side, 206.7 m by 10 m, with its balustrade. Exact terrace detail is schematic.
explanations.main roof: The main pitched roof of the palace behind the river front. Exact roof profile is schematic.
explanations.roof chimneys: Chimney stacks along the main roof. About four hundred fires burned around the palace. Exact stack positions are schematic.
explanations.frontage pinnacles: Pinnacles rising between the window bays along the frontage, enlivening the skyline. Exact pinnacle shapes are schematic.
explanations.westminster hall: Westminster Hall, the oldest structure on the estate, completed in 1099, 20.7 m by 73.2 m, saved from the 1834 fire by firefighting efforts and a change in the wind.
explanations.westminster hall roof: The hammerbeam roof of Westminster Hall, the largest medieval timber roof in Northern Europe. Exact timber work is schematic.
explanations.westminster hall porches: The north and south porches of Westminster Hall. Exact porch detail is schematic.
explanations.cromwell statue: The bronze statue of Oliver Cromwell on Cromwell Green, erected amid controversy in 1899. Exact statue is schematic.
explanations.new palace yard: New Palace Yard on the north side of the palace, private and closed to the public. Exact layout is schematic.
explanations.old palace yard: Old Palace Yard in front of the palace, paved over and covered in concrete security blocks. Exact layout is schematic.
explanations.cromwell green: Cromwell Green outside Westminster Hall. Exact layout is schematic.
explanations.palace courtyards: The internal courtyards of the palace: Speakers Court, State Officers Court and Royal Court. Exact layouts are schematic.
explanations.black rods garden: Black Rods Garden, named after the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, closed to the public and used as a private entrance. Exact layout is schematic.
explanations.victoria tower gardens: Victoria Tower Gardens, a public park along the river south of the palace. Exact layout is schematic.
explanations.speakers green: Speakers Green, directly north of the palace, private and closed to the public. Exact layout is schematic.
explanations.college green: College Green opposite the House of Lords, commonly used for television interviews with politicians. Exact layout is schematic.
